title: Elevator Manufacturer
prompt: Your client is a 40-year-old elevator manufacturer in India. Historically they make almost everything in-house: cabins, doors, rails and so on. Over the last couple of years they have started facing manufacturing-related challenges, and the CEO has asked for your help.

facts.asks: Demand side, or supply and internal operations
facts.reveal: Demand has been stable and customer satisfaction on quality remains strong.

facts.asks: Industry-wide or specific to the client
facts.reveal: The issues are internal and specific to the company.
Over the last two years procurement costs have gone up by roughly 20%, and factory utilisation has become uneven: some processes are heavily bottlenecked while some lines are underused.

Mechanical assemblies (rails, guide systems, pulleys, drive mechanisms); electrical and electronics (control panels, PCB boards, wiring assemblies, sensors); and metal structures (cabin bodies, doors, frames, safety enclosures).
Currently 90% of these are manufactured in-house, because "we always did it that way".

For metal frames and cabins, external suppliers are 25% cheaper at the same quality. For control systems and safety assemblies, vendors exist but supply is concentrated and expensive; internal production is already competitive.

facts.asks: After the candidate proposes a make-or-buy split
facts.reveal: It looks fine, but can you please elaborate your approach?
Can you quantify the potential savings, for example for metal fabrication? Make genuine assumptions as required.

facts.asks: In-house operations and where the bottlenecks are
facts.reveal: There are bottlenecks at two main places: the motor assembly line, which is slower and requires skilled labour, and the final testing station, where testing takes a long time. Meanwhile cabins are being produced faster and piling up in inventory.

facts.asks: Anything else, after the bottleneck fixes
facts.reveal: There is one additional problem: the inventory sitting period is high. What are your suggestions for it?

acceptedAssumptions: Metal fabrication is about 35% of material cost
Material cost is about 50% of revenue

crux.statement: One legacy habit causes two problems. Make or buy: outsource high-volume, non-differentiating metal fabrication and keep safety and control systems in-house; segment categories, judge total cost rather than unit price, and move from spot buying to performance-linked contracts. Line imbalance: cabins outrun the motor and testing constraints, so faster cabin output only builds inventory.
crux.clue: "Cabins are being produced faster and piling up in inventory."
crux.test: Remove "25% cheaper, same quality" and the make-or-buy call has no basis. Remove the cabin pile-up and the bottleneck reads as a capacity shortage.

paths: Procurement optimisation → production and factory efficiency → inventory (the source's route)
Start from the shop floor, then reach make-or-buy

wrongTurns.text: Building a new plant or adding capacity

quant.working: 0.25 × 0.35 = 8.75% off material cost. Material is about 50% of revenue, so 8.75% × 0.5 = about 4.4 percentage points of margin. The source says 4–5 points.
quant.answer: About 8.75% of material cost, or about 4.4 percentage points of margin

answerKey: Outsource metal cabins and frames selectively; keep strategic and supply-risky items in-house
Bottlenecks: schedule cabins to the motor and testing constraint, add test rigs, cross-train labour, preventive maintenance on the motor line
Inventory: segment by criticality, sales and operations planning, forecast-based buying, vendor-managed inventory for standard parts, which frees working capital

close.condition: The candidate has addressed both procurement and the line imbalance.
close.prompt: What are your final recommendations for the owner?

anchors.s7: The make-or-buy split plus the savings maths.
anchors.s9: Both problems, with the bottleneck logic stated (throughput is set by the constraint), the saving quantified, and the inventory and working-capital link made.
